I am 76 years old, and I have farmed in Quzhou County on the North China Plain for more than fifty years. Unlike most men of my generation here, I finished senior high school, and over the decades I have read the agricultural bulletins from the China Agricultural University research station in our county. I understand soil fertility and plant nutrition, but I am also practical — at my age, I cannot take big risks or work myself to exhaustion.

It is early spring now, and my winter wheat is already in the ground, sown last October after rotary tillage. I keep all 10 of my mu in the wheat-maize double-cropping rotation. It is the most reliable system in our county — two harvests a year, and the grain station always purchases wheat. I stopped growing cotton years ago. The picking is too much bending for an old man, and the market price jumps around too much.

For the wheat, I plant about 15 kg per mu of improved seed — not the old local varieties, but ones I have selected over the years that resist lodging and disease. My basal fertilizer is compound, about 50 kg per mu with an 18-22-5 formula, and I will topdress with urea at jointing in early April. Altogether that is about 18 kg of nitrogen, 11 kg of phosphorus, and 3 kg of potassium per mu. I will irrigate four times — winter, green-up, jointing, and grain filling — because groundwater irrigation is costly with the electric pumps, but you cannot skip it if you want a decent stand. I plan four pesticide sprays: herbicide once before winter, insecticide twice in spring for aphids, and a fungicide at heading if the humidity rises. I expect around 500 kg per mu from the wheat if the spring weather holds.

For summer maize, I will plant hybrid seed — Nongda or Denghai, one package per mu — immediately after wheat harvest in early June. There is no time for tillage; we direct-seed into the wheat stubble with no-tillage, which also saves fuel and labor at a critical moment when the turnaround is barely a week. I will put down compound fertilizer at planting, about 40 kg per mu of 28-6-6, which gives roughly 11 kg nitrogen, 3 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium per mu. The maize will need two irrigations in summer and three pesticide sprays for weeds and corn borers. I expect about 550 kg per mu.

I could push for higher yields with more fertilizer, but I learned long ago that the extra input cost often does not pay back on these soils, and at 76 I want a steady, manageable system rather than chasing every last kilogram.
